title: Clinical and virological characterisation of Oropouche, dengue, and chikungunya during simultaneous co-circulation in the State of Espírito Santo, Brazil: a retrospective observational study

license.text: This is an open access article under the CC BY-NC license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/).

paragraphs.en: We searched PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science from inception to March 2026 for studies comparing clinical or virological characteristics of OROV, DENV, and CHIKV in co-endemic or co-circulating settings. Search terms included “Oropouche virus”, “dengue”, “chikungunya”, “clinical characteristics”, “viral load”, “Ct values”, “co circulation”, “co-endemic”, and “comparative study”, without language restrictions. While recent large-scale epidemiological studies from southeastern Brazil have compared OROV and DENV infection clinical profiles, showing substantial clinical overlap alongside differences in severity and epidemiological patterns, studies integrating clinical phenotyping with viral load dynamics across OROV, DENV, and CHIKV infections simultaneously remain scarce. Evidence on OROV has been derived predominantly from outbreak investigations in the Amazon basin, with more recent clinical and laboratory characterisations emerging from southeastern Brazil, although clinical characterisation in urban or co-endemic contexts remains limited. For DENV, higher viral loads have been associated with increased severity and specific manifestations, though findings are inconsistent across settings. For CHIKV, viral load has been associated with acute symptom intensity, but comparative data across co-circulating arboviruses remain limited. Musculoskeletal predominance in CHIKV and gastrointestinal manifestations in DENV have been described, but their adjusted associations with arboviral infectionin co endemic settings — where all three viruses present as acute febrile illness — remains incompletely quantified.

Building on previous comparative studies, our study provides three complementary advances. First, we extend the comparative framework to include CHIKV, the primary clinical mimic of OROV-associated arthralgia, allowing estimation of adjusted associations between musculoskeletal symptoms and arboviral infection. Second, beyond comparing isolated symptom frequencies, we characterized the internal structure of symptom co-occurrence, showing distinct patterns of symptom co-occurrence across infections, providing descriptive information on multidimensional clinical presentation. Finally, we provide, to our knowledge, a detailed characterization of cross-sectional Ct value patterns in a large urban OROV cohort and demonstrate that associations between standardized Ct values and clinical phenotypes differ substantially across arboviruses. Crucially, we identified consistent associations between Ct values and systemic and musculoskeletal clinical phenotypes in OROV that were not observed in the other two infections.

sections.title: Implications of all the available evidence

paragraphs.en: As OROV continues to expand beyond its historical Amazonian range into urban centers with established DENV and CHIKV transmission, accurate clinical differentiation is increasingly critical for patient management, surveillance attribution, and diagnostic resource allocation. The clinical and virological patterns identified here provide descriptive foundations that may inform future development of probabilistic diagnostic algorithms applicable in resource-limited settings where laboratory confirmation is delayed. Such algorithms would require formal predictive modelling, prospective validation, and assessment across diverse epidemiological and health system contexts. The observed non-monotonic population-level Ct pattern of OROV suggests that the temporal distribution of detectable viral RNA in OROV differs from the overall pattern observed for DENV and CHIKV. However, because these findings derive from cross sectional rather than longitudinal sampling, the underlying biological mechanisms remain uncertain and require prospective investigation.

The 2024–2025 expansion of Oropouche virus (OROV) into southeastern Brazil marks one of the largest outbreaks of this Amazonian pathogen documented to date.1 In Espírito Santo state, OROV co-circulated with dengue (DENV) and chikungunya (CHIKV) virus,2 creating considerable diagnostic complexity: all three viruses present with overlapping acute febrile syndromes that are difficult to distinguish clinically without laboratory confirmation.3,4 While DENV and CHIKV are well-established in Latin America,5 OROV has recently expanded beyond its historically endemic range, intensifying both the frequency of outbreaks and the challenges of clinical and epidemiological management in co-endemic settings.4,5

In this context, syndromic diagnosis remains insufficient. Dengue, chikungunya, and Oropouche commonly present as acute febrile illnesses with overlapping clinical manifestations, including fever, headache, myalgia, and arthralgia.6, 7, 8, 9 Despite some characteristic features — such as prominent musculoskeletal involvement in chikungunya8 and more frequent gastrointestinal or retro-orbital manifestations in dengue7 — substantial clinical overlap persists. This overlap limits the accuracy of syndromic diagnosis and complicates clinical decision-making, particularly in resource-limited settings where laboratory confirmation may not be readily available. This is consistent with previous epidemiological studies showing overlapping clinical presentations between Oropouche and dengue in co-circulating settings.9 Accurate differentiation has become particularly urgent as vaccines emerge for DENV and CHIKV5 — interventions that remain unavailable for OROV.

Recent reports have also raised concerns about the occurrence of severe manifestations associated with OROV infection, including neurological involvement,10 fatal outcomes,11 and possible congenital complications,12 highlighting the broader clinical spectrum of this emerging arbovirus. Within the acute febrile presentation that characterizes the majority of cases in co-endemic settings, emerging evidence suggests that arboviral infections may also differ in their multidimensional clinical phenotypes and symptom clustering patterns, reflecting distinct underlying pathophysiological processes.13,14 However, comparative analyses integrating these dimensions across multiple co-circulating arboviruses remain limited, particularly for OROV, whose clinical characterization outside the Amazon region is still evolving.15 The present study addresses this gap by focusing on the comparative structure of acute clinical phenotypes and their virological correlates during simultaneous co-circulation.

Viral load represents a potentially important, yet underexplored, dimension of this clinical heterogeneity. Cycle threshold (Ct) values obtained by RT-PCR are widely used as an imperfect but practical proxy for viral load,2,16 with lower Ct values indicating higher levels of viral RNA. In dengue, higher viral loads have been associated with increased disease severity and specific clinical manifestations,17,18 although this relationship is heterogeneous and influenced by host and viral factors.19 For chikungunya, available evidence suggests a possible association between viral load and symptom intensity during the acute phase.20,21

For OROV, however, this relationship remains poorly understood. Recent findings2 suggest that lower Ct values may be associated with key systemic symptoms such as fever, headache, and myalgia. Additionally, reports of fatal cases with low Ct values and rapid clinical progression raise concerns about a possible link between viral burden and disease severity.11 Emerging longitudinal evidence further indicates that OROV may exhibit prolonged viral RNA detection, with evidence of ongoing replication across multiple body compartments22 suggesting distinct viral dynamics compared to other arboviruses.

Understanding how viral load relates to clinical expression in co-endemic settings may provide additional insights into the clinical characterization of arboviral infections and guiding diagnostic strategies. Moreover, integrating clinical and virological data may help identify distinguishing patterns that are not apparent when considering these dimensions separately. Therefore, this study aimed to: (a) compare the clinical and epidemiological characteristics of DENV, CHIKV, and OROV infections in a co-endemic setting; (b) characterize the internal structure of symptom co-occurrence as a multidimensional phenotype; and (c) explore the integration of cross-sectional Ct value patterns with clinical expression. These objectives are sequential: clinical comparison establishes the baseline differences, phenotyping reveals how symptoms organise within each infection, and virological analysis assesses whether molecular patterns are associated with differences in clinical expression. This framework is intended to advance understanding rather than establish validated clinical rules.

We conducted a retrospective observational study using routinely collected surveillance and laboratory data from the State of Espírito Santo, Brazil, from Jan 1, 2024, to Dec 31, 2025. Data were obtained from the Laboratory Environment Manager (Gerenciador de Ambiente Laboratorial–GAL), which records laboratory-confirmed arboviral diagnoses, and the e-SUS Notifica platform (Brazil's Electronic Unified Health System Notification system), which aggregates epidemiological and clinical reports of suspected cases. Sex was recorded in the surveillance database as male or female and was analysed as a biological sex variable. Information on gender identity was not collected or available in the databases used for this study.

To ensure comparability, only serum samples were included. This restriction was applied uniformly across all arboviruses to minimise variability introduced by differences in biological compartment (eg, viral RNA concentration, inhibitor profiles, and pre-analytical handling), which could confound comparisons of temporal and clinical patterns. Although OROV RNA may persist longer in other body fluids, serum was the only biological specimen consistently available for all three arboviruses within the surveillance system, allowing direct comparison across infections. Records from GAL and e-SUS were linked using deterministic matching based on patient name, date of birth, and mother's name. After linkage, all data were de-identified. Eligible participants were residents of Espírito Santo State with RT-qPCR-confirmed DENV, CHIKV, or OROV infection and a corresponding matched notification. We excluded unmatched records, discordant entries, co-infections, and duplicate notifications (retaining one record per individual per year).

Ct values were retrieved from an internal laboratory database and merged with the linked dataset. All RT-qPCR assays were performed at the state reference laboratory (LACEN-ES) using standardised protocols. Molecular assays, amplification conditions, target genes, and positivity thresholds are summarized in Supplementary Table S1. Results were interpreted according to the assay-specific positivity thresholds (Ct ≤ 40 for the commercial DENV/CHIKV/ZIKV assays and Ct ≤ 38 for the OROV assay; Supplementary Table S1). Ct values were recorded only for detectable samples. Samples were initially tested by multiplex RT-qPCR for DENV, CHIKV, and ZIKV; samples with non-detectable results meeting surveillance criteria were subsequently tested for OROV. Cases without Ct values were excluded (n = 139; DENV: 71, CHIKV: 17, OROV: 51), reflecting incomplete capture during manual curation of the secondary database rather than laboratory analytical failure. Analyses were restricted to complete-case data. The proportion and distribution of missing data across arboviral groups and variables are detailed in Supplementary Table S2 and Fig. 1.

Missingness was primarily related to incomplete linkage between surveillance and laboratory databases and absence of Ct values for a small proportion of laboratory-confirmed cases. Given the low proportion of missing data, a complete-case analysis was performed (Supplementary Table S2), which was considered unlikely to substantially bias the effect estimates. Nevertheless, we acknowledge that exclusion of cases with missing data may introduce selection bias, and findings should be interpreted accordingly. No formal sample size calculation was performed, as this was a population-based study. The final analytical dataset comprised 10,793 infections (4058 DENV, 2508 CHIKV, and 4227 OROV).

Descriptive analyses were conducted to summarise epidemiological, clinical, and laboratory characteristics of arboviral infections. Continuous variables were reported as medians with interquartile ranges (IQRs), whereas categorical variables were expressed as counts and percentages. Comparisons across DENV, CHIKV, and OROV groups were performed using the Kruskal–Wallis test for continuous variables and the χ2 test for categorical variables. When expected cell counts were fewer than five, p values were estimated using Monte Carlo simulation. All tests were two-sided.

Patterns of symptom co-occurrence were assessed using pairwise phi (ϕ) coefficients, a measure of association specifically designed for binary variables. The false discovery rate (FDR) approach was selected because the analyses involved multiple related symptom comparisons and clinical domains. Unlike family-wise error rate procedures such as the Bonferroni correction, which can be overly conservative and reduce power when tests are correlated, FDR controls the expected proportion of false discoveries among statistically significant findings while retaining greater power for exploratory analyses. Given the exploratory nature of the symptom co-occurrence and clinical-domain analyses, FDR was considered appropriate.

To identify clinical features independently associated with each arboviral infection, multinomial logistic regression models were fitted with arbovirus type (DENV, CHIKV, OROV) as the outcome. Models were adjusted for age, sex, and time since symptom onset (days). To facilitate pairwise comparisons, models were refitted using alternative reference categories. Results are presented as odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs). All symptoms available and consistently recorded across the three arboviral surveillance datasets were included as candidate clinical variables in the multinomial models.

Cycle threshold (Ct) values, obtained from RT-qPCR assays, provide a semi-quantitative proxy of viral RNA levels and may be influenced by pre-analytical and analytical factors; therefore, they should be interpreted as relative rather than absolute measures of viral load.

To account for differences in Ct distributions across arboviruses, Ct values were standardised within each virus group using z-score transformation (mean 0, SD 1). All analyses involving Ct values were conducted within each virus group, and no direct comparisons of Ct values between arboviruses were performed. Associations between viral load and clinical expression were evaluated using linear regression models with Ct z-scores as continuous predictors. Analyses were stratified by virus (DENV, CHIKV, and OROV) and adjusted for age, sex, and time since symptom onset (days). Effect estimates are presented as regression coefficients (β) with 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs). To account for multiple comparisons across clinical domains, p values were adjusted using the FDR method.

sections.title: Clinical domain scores and association with Ct values

paragraphs.en: To investigate the relationship between viral load and clinical expression, symptom domains were defined a priori based on clinical relevance and established syndromic groupings in arboviral infections, including systemic (fever, headache), gastrointestinal (nausea, vomiting), musculoskeletal (myalgia, arthritis, intense arthralgia), localised pain (back pain, retro-orbital pain), and mucocutaneous (rash, petechiae, conjunctivitis) domains. This approach was intended to capture higher-order patterns of symptom organisation beyond individual manifestations.

For each participant, domain-specific scores were calculated as the proportion of symptoms present within each domain, ranging from 0 to 1. A global clinical score was defined as the mean of all domain scores. These composite measures were designed as exploratory indicators of multidimensional clinical phenotype rather than validated severity scales, and were used to facilitate comparison of clinical expression across arboviruses in a standardised manner.

Associations between Ct values and clinical domain scores were evaluated using multivariable linear regression models stratified by virus (DENV, CHIKV, and OROV). Ct values were modelled as continuous variables after standardisation within each virus (z-scores). All models were adjusted for age, sex, and time since symptom onset, with the latter modelled using restricted natural cubic splines (three degrees of freedom) to account for potential non-linear effects. Effect estimates are presented as regression coefficients (β) with 95% confidence intervals. To account for multiple comparisons across symptom domains, p values were adjusted using the false discovery rate (FDR) method.

All statistical analyses were performed in R (version 4·4·3). Data processing and visualisation were conducted using established packages within the R ecosystem, including tidyverse (data manipulation), dplyr and tidyr (data wrangling), broom (model outputs), purrr (functional programming), and ggplot2 (visualisation).

This study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. Ethical approval was granted by the Human Research Ethics Committee of the University of Vila Velha (Comitê de Ética em Pesquisa da Universidade de Vila Velha; CAAE no. 84698324·7·0000·5064). Given the retrospective design of the study and the use of de-identified routine surveillance data, the requirement for individual informed consent was waived by the approving ethics committee. All data were de-identified prior to analysis, and no procedures were performed on human participants beyond the collection of routinely available diagnostic and surveillance records.
The funders had no role in the study design; collection, analysis, or interpretation of the data; writing of the report; or the decision to submit the manuscript for publication.

After deterministic linkage of surveillance and laboratory databases and application of predefined exclusion criteria (Fig. 1; Supplementary Table S2), the final analytical dataset comprised 10,793 laboratory-confirmed cases, including 4058 DENV, 2508 CHIKV, and 4227 OROV infections. These cases were identified over a 24-month period characterised by sequential epidemic waves, with DENV predominating in early 2024, CHIKV in mid-2024, and OROV in late 2024 through early 2025 (Fig. 2A). Despite temporal variation in predominance, substantial temporal overlap enabled direct comparisons: all three viruses co-circulated in 41% of epidemiological weeks, and at least two viruses were present in 83% of weeks (Supplementary Table S3).

Cases were geographically widespread but exhibited distinct clustering patterns, with DENV concentrated in central–northern regions, OROV in central–southern areas, and CHIKV more spatially restricted (Fig. 2B). Demographically, OROV infections occurred in older individuals (median age 49 years [IQR 43–56]) compared with CHIKV (44 [28–59]) and DENV (35 [19–51]; p < 0·0001), and the proportion of female cases differed across infections, being highest in CHIKV(1402/2508 [55·9%]), followed by DENV (2039/4058 [50·2%]) and OROV (2050/4227 [48·5%]; p < 0·0001) (Table 1; Fig. 2C).

Clear differences in clinical presentation were observed across arboviral infections (Table 1). OROV cases were characterised by a high prevalence of systemic symptoms, including fever (n = 4134, 97·8%), headache (n = 4068, 96·2%), and myalgia (n = 3760, 89·0%), alongside a high frequency of intense arthralgia (n = 3653, 86·4%). In contrast, CHIKV infections exhibited a predominantly musculoskeletal-inflammatory profile, with higher frequencies of arthritis (n = 726, 28·9%), rash (n = 359, 14·3%), petechiae (n = 224, 8·9%), and conjunctivitis (n = 99, 3·9%) than DENV or OROV. DENV presented an intermediate profile, combining systemic manifestations with higher frequencies of gastrointestinal and pain-related symptoms, particularly nausea (n = 1785, 44·0%), vomiting (n = 831, 20·5%), back pain (n = 1564, 38·5%), and retro-orbital pain (n = 1871, 46·1%). When stratified by serotype, broadly similar clinical profiles were observed between DENV1 and DENV2, with modest differences in selected symptoms, including higher frequencies of gastrointestinal manifestations in DENV2. Detailed comparisons are provided in Supplementary Table S4.

Beyond differences in symptom frequencies, symptom co-occurrence revealed distinct patterns across arboviral infections (Supplementary Figure S1). CHIKV showed the most cohesive co-occurrence pattern, characterised by tightly clustered musculoskeletal manifestations. DENV exhibited a more structured pattern centred on gastrointestinal and pain-related symptoms, whereas OROV exhibited a comparatively diffuse network with fewer dominant symptoms clusters. These findings suggest that the three arboviruses differ not only in individual symptom prevalence but also in the overall pattern of symptom co-occurrence. When these features were assessed jointly in multinomial logistic regression models, several clinical features remained independently associated with arboviral infection (Fig. 3). In multinomial logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, and time since symptom onset, arthritis was positively associated with CHIKV versus OROV (OR 5·22 [95% CI 4·08–6·68]), as was rash (2·39 [1·83–3·12]). Conversely, nausea (2·98 [2·52–3·53]), vomiting (2·54 [2·01–3·21]), and retro-orbital pain (8·00 [6·69–9·56]) were positively associated with DENV versus OROV. Intense arthralgia was inversely associated with CHIKV versus OROV (0·39 [0·34–0·45]) and DENV versus OROV (0·07 [0·06–0·08]). Direct comparison between CHIKV and DENV reinforced these distinctions, with CHIKV remaining associated with joint-related manifestations and DENV with gastrointestinal features.

Sex-specific analyses revealed that heterogeneous associations between sex and clinical manifestations varied across arboviruses (Supplementary Table S5). In DENV, female sex was positively associated with headache (OR 1·46, 95% CI 1·22–1·74), nausea (1·62, 1·43–1·84), vomiting (1·22, 1·04–1·42), and petechiae (1·52, 1·16–2·01), whereas fever was inversely associated with female sex (0·69, 0·56–0·84). In CHIKV, female sex was positively associated with intense arthralgia (1·53, 1·30–1·79), nausea (1·49, 1·26–1·76), petechiae (1·46, 1·09–1·95), retro-orbital pain (1·34, 1·14–1·58), and arthritis (1·23, 1·03–1·47), whereas myalgia was inversely associated with female sex (0·77, 0·64–0·92). No statistically significant associations between female sex and individual symptoms were observed for OROV after adjustment for age.

Ct values, used as a semi-quantitative proxy for viral RNA levels, differed across arboviral infections (Fig. 4). Descriptive statistics of raw Ct values by virus were: OROV median 23·6 [IQR 20·7–27·4], DENV 25·8 [22·1–30·2], and CHIKV 26·4 [22·5–31·3]. Despite these differences, Ct distributions overlapped substantially across infections, indicating considerable inter-individual variability (Fig. 4). When examined in relation to time since symptom onset, DENV and CHIKV showed an overall increase in cross-sectional Ct values over time, consistent with declining detectable viral RNA, although day-to-day variability was observed. OROV showed a non-monotonic population-level pattern, with an initial rise in Ct values between days 3 and 5 followed by lower values after day 7, suggesting heterogeneous viral RNA kinetics at the population level (Fig. 4A–C).

To investigate the relationship between viral load and clinical presentation, Ct values were standardised within each infection (z-scores) and analysed in relation to domain-specific clinical phenotype scores using multivariable linear regression models adjusted for age, sex, and days since symptom onset (Fig. 4D). Clinical domain scores showed heterogeneous distributions (Supplementary Table S6), with systemic scores concentrated near the upper bound of the scale, mucocutaneous scores concentrated near zero, and the global score displaying an intermediate distribution.

In DENV, a small positive association between standardised Ct values and the mucocutaneous domain was observed, whereas estimates for the other clinical domains were close to the null. In CHIKV, no statistically significant associations between standardised Ct values and the clinical domain scores were observed after adjustment and FDR correction (Fig. 4D). In contrast, OROV infection showed consistent associations between viral load and clinical expression. Among patients with OROV infection, lower standardised Ct values (reflecting higher viral load) were independently associated with higher systemic (β −0·008 [95% CI −0·012 to −0·004]; p = 0·0001), musculoskeletal (β −0·015 [−0·020 to −0·009]; p < 0·0001), and global clinical phenotype scores (β −0·004 [−0·006 to −0·002]; p = 0·0031). Conversely, higher Ct values were associated with slightly higher mucocutaneous scores (β 0·005 [0·002 to 0·007]; p = 0·0015) (Supplementary Table S7). Although statistically significant, the magnitude of these associations was modest, indicating that viral load explained only a limited proportion of the observed variability in clinical presentation. These associations remained robust after adjustment and correction for multiple comparisons.

In this large-scale comparative analysis conducted during simultaneous circulation of dengue, chikungunya, and Oropouche in the State of Espírito Santo, Brazil, we identified three major findings that advance our understanding of arboviral syndromes in co-endemic settings. First, although the three arboviral infections showed substantial overlap in acute febrile presentation, they differed consistently in the frequency and combination of clinical manifestations. On average, chikungunya cases showed a predominance of musculoskeletal-inflammatory manifestations, dengue cases more frequently presented gastrointestinal symptoms and localized pain, whereas Oropouche cases were characterized by a predominantly systemic febrile presentation with diffuse musculoskeletal symptoms but fewer objective inflammatory manifestations. Second, we showed that these infections differed not only in individual symptom frequencies but also in their patterns of co-occurrence, indicating differences in the organisation of clinical manifestations. Third, whereas Ct values showed little association with clinical phenotype in dengue and chikungunya, lower standardised Ct values in Oropouche infection were consistently associated with greater systemic and musculoskeletal clinical expression.

Our findings align with and extend previous evidence from southeastern Brazil showing substantial clinical overlap between Oropouche and dengue, alongside distinct epidemiological and severity profiles.9 While these studies demonstrated important differences in symptom frequencies and outcomes, they did not integrate multivariable clinical associations with virological data. By combining multivariable clinical modelling with viral load dynamics, our study provides a more refined characterisation of arboviral phenotypes in co-endemic settings. The musculoskeletal predominance of chikungunya is well documented and has been consistently recognised since the epidemics in La Réunion (2005–2006)23 and later in the Americas,24 where polyarthralgia and arthritis emerged as defining clinical features. Similarly, gastrointestinal and retro-orbital manifestations have long been recognised in dengue,7 although their specific association patternsin co-endemic settings has remained incompletely quantified.3,14 For Oropouche, by contrast, earlier clinical descriptions were derived predominantly from outbreaks in the Amazon basin,4 where laboratory access was more limited and direct comparison with simultaneously co-circulating dengue and chikungunya was generally not possible. Building on previous comparative studies, this work integrates clinical phenotyping with analyses of viral RNA levels across laboratory-confirmed OROV, DENV, and CHIKV infections during co-circulation. The substantial overlap in clinical presentation highlights the limitations of symptom-based clinical assessment alone and underscores the need for updated clinical frameworks as this pathogen expands beyond its historical range.1,4

Chikungunya showed the most distinct musculoskeletal-inflammatory phenotype, characterised by higher frequencies of arthritis, rash, and conjunctivitis — features that remained associated with CHIKV after adjustment for age, sex, and time since symptom onset. This pattern is consistent with the recognised tropism of arthritogenic alphaviruses for synovial and musculoskeletal tissues, in which macrophage-rich inflammatory infiltrates play a central role in disease pathogenesis.25 Previous outbreak and cohort studies have similarly identified polyarthralgia and arthritis as key distinguishing features of CHIKV infection,23,24 supporting the consistency of our findings across different epidemiological settings. The stronger symptom clustering observed in our analyses further suggests a conserved clinical syndrome across patients and epidemiological settings. Sex-stratified analyses supported this pattern: female patients with CHIKV had significantly higher odds of having intense arthralgia and arthritis after adjustment for age, whereas no comparable sex-related differences in musculoskeletal manifestations were observed in OROV. This asymmetry is consistent with previous evidence that women experience a greater burden of persistent chikungunya arthropathy.26 Sex-related differences in host inflammatory responses might contribute,8 although differences in healthcare-seeking behaviour cannot be excluded from surveillance-based data.

After adjustment for age, sex, and time since symptom onset, nausea, vomiting, retro-orbital pain, and back pain were positively associated with Dengue relative to the other arboviral infections. These findings are consistent with the well-described clinical manifestations of dengue, which include gastrointestinal symptoms and retro-orbital pain during the acute phase.19,27 Retro-orbital pain, in particular, is a long-recognised clinical feature of dengue19 and its persistence as a significant adjusted association in our models in our models supports its continued inclusion in syndromic case definitions. Although DENV-2 was associated with higher frequencies of vomiting, nausea, and intense arthralgia compared with DENV-1 in our cohort, these differences were modest and, together with conflicting serotype-specific symptom profiles reported elsewhere,28 reinforce that symptom profiles are unreliable indicators of specific serotypes in routine co-endemic settings. This finding is relevant to clinicians, who often rely on clinical presentation in the absence of laboratory typing.

Oropouche, by contrast, combined near-universal fever and headache with a high frequency of intense arthralgia and myalgia, aligned with recent reports,9 including detailed clinical and laboratory characterisations of OROV infection as a predominantly systemic febrile illness,15 yet lacked the objective inflammatory signature of arthritis and rash that characterises chikungunya.23,24 This dissociation — prominent arthralgia in the absence of objective inflammatory signs — indicates that the clinical presentation of OROV differs from that of CHIKV despite overlap in musculoskeletal symptoms. Previous immunological studies have reported that inflammatory responses during OROV infection are not closely correlated with RNA levels,29 which may contribute to the distinct clinical presentation observed in comparison with CHIKV.25 This interpretation is consistent with prior studies describing diffuse musculoskeletal symptoms in OROV infection without clear focal inflammatory manifestations.15 Adjusted models confirmed the non-specific clinical profile of Oropouche, with no symptom showing a strong independent association. This was most evident for intense arthralgia: despite its high prevalence and higher frequency than in CHIKV or DENV infections, its adjusted association was weak. This underscores the distinction between symptom frequency and diagnostic value. Clinically, intense arthralgia should not exclude OROV infection, whereas its absence may be more informative in co-endemic settings.

Virologically, OROV infection exhibited greater temporal variability in Ct values across days since symptom onset than DENV and CHIKV, resulting in a non-monotonic cross-sectional pattern. However, this pattern could reflect sampling heterogeneity (late presenters with higher viral loads), healthcare-seeking behaviour, or true biological variability in a subset of individuals. Longitudinal intra-individual sampling is required to distinguish these alternatives. Nevertheless, this temporal variability is compatible with previous reports describing prolonged detection of OROV RNA in some patients.22 The observed heterogeneity has practical implications for molecular diagnosis, suggesting that RT-PCR results should always be interpreted in the context of the timing of sample collection.30 Whereas DENV and CHIKV showed limited associations between viral load and clinical phenotype, OROV showed consistent associations between lower Ct values and higher systemic, musculoskeletal, and global clinical scores after adjustment. Although effect sizes were modest, this finding suggests a stronger association between relative viral RNA levels and clinical expression in OROV, whereas in DENV and CHIKV, manifestations appear less directly related to viral load at the time of sampling.19,20 This distinction has practical implications: in OROV infection, a low Ct value may reflect not only diagnostic positivity but also greater symptom burden, whereas in DENV and CHIKV infection, Ct values alone are unlikely to capture clinical severity.

Taken together, these findings indicate that arboviral infections differ not only in clinical phenotype and symptom structure but also in the relationship between viral RNA levels and clinical expression. While associations between Ct values and clinical phenotype were limited in dengue and not statistically significant after adjustment and FDR correction in chikungunya, Oropouche showed a more consistent association between lower Ct values and greater systemic and musculoskeletal clinical expression. These findings suggest distinct clinical–virological relationships across the three arboviruses, although the cross-sectional design precludes inference about temporal or causal relationships between viral load and symptom manifestation.

These findings are directly relevant to surveillance and patient care in co-endemic settings, where laboratory capacity may become constrained during epidemic surges and clinicians often rely on syndromic evaluation. Our results suggest that combinations of arthritis and rash are more frequently associated with CHIKV infection, whereas nausea, vomiting, and retro-orbital pain are more frequently associated with DENV infection. Likewise, a predominantly systemic febrile presentation with diffuse arthralgia but without objective inflammatory signs may increase the clinical suspicion of OROV, particularly in newly affected regions and among older patients. These patterns should be interpreted as probabilistic clinical features rather than diagnostic criteria and require external validation before being incorporated into clinical decision-making algorithms. Because laboratory-confirmed arboviral co-infections were excluded, the clinical patterns described here should be interpreted as applying to single-virus infections. Nevertheless, when considered alongside molecular testing and local epidemiological context, they may assist clinical assessment and surveillance activities in co-endemic settings. As DENV vaccines are being implemented in Brazil31 and CHIKV vaccines progress toward broader deployment,32 improved differentiation between vaccine-breakthrough dengue or chikungunya and incident OROV infection will become increasingly important for clinical management and surveillance.

This study has several limitations. First, the retrospective, cross-sectional design precludes causal inference regarding the relationship between viral RNA levels and clinical outcomes. Although time since symptom onset was incorporated into all analyses using restricted natural cubic splines, residual confounding due to variation in sampling time cannot be excluded. Second, exclusion of cases with missing Ct values or incomplete database linkage may have introduced selection bias, although exclusion rates were low and similar across arboviruses. Third, clinical information was derived from routine surveillance records and is therefore subject to reporting variability and incomplete symptom ascertainment. In addition, temporal changes in healthcare-seeking behaviour, laboratory demand, and surveillance practices during successive epidemic waves may have influenced case ascertainment and the probability of laboratory confirmation across viruses. Fourth, Ct values are an indirect proxy for viral RNA levels and cannot be directly compared across arboviruses because different virus-specific RT-qPCR assays were used, despite standardized testing at the same state reference laboratory. Accordingly, all inferential analyses involving Ct values were performed after within-virus standardization. Fifth, the clinical presentations identified here represent laboratory-confirmed single-virus infections and should be interpreted as probabilistic clinical patterns rather than validated diagnostic tools. Because the study was designed to explain clinical differences rather than develop prediction models, no external validation or assessment of diagnostic performance was performed. Sixth, the unavailability of data on race, ethnicity, gender identity, and treatment received prior to sample collection limited our ability to assess these factors as potential sources of residual confounding. Although biological sex was recorded as male or female and included in the analyses, information on gender identity was not available. Sociodemographic factors may influence healthcare-seeking behaviour and exposure patterns, whereas prior clinical management may affect symptom reporting and the timing of sample collection. The absence of these variables may therefore have contributed to residual confounding and may restrict the generalisability of our findings. Finally, although this study was conducted in a single Brazilian state, Espírito Santo experienced sustained co-circulation of DENV, CHIKV, and OROV under standardized laboratory surveillance, providing a unique setting for comparative analyses that may be informative for other tropical regions experiencing OROV emergence.

In conclusion, co-circulating DENV, CHIKV, and OROV in the State of Espírito Santo, Brazil exhibited distinct clinical presentations and patterns of symptom co-occurrence, with specific clinical manifestations showing adjusted associations with individual arboviral infections. Arthritis and rash were positively associated with CHIKV relative to OROV, whereas nausea, vomiting, and retro-orbital pain were positively associated with DENV. OROV was characterised by frequent systemic and musculoskeletal manifestations and showed associations between lower standardised Ct values and greater systemic and musculoskeletal clinical scores. These findings provide comparative evidence on clinical and virological patterns during arboviral co-circulation but should not be interpreted as validated diagnostic rules.

figures.label: Fig. 1
figures.caption: Flowchart of dataset construction and participant selection stratified by arbovirus. Records were retrieved from the Laboratory Environment Manager (GAL; RT-PCR-confirmed cases only) and e-SUS Notifica (epidemiological notifications) for the period 2024–2025, linked through deterministic matching based on patient name, date of birth, and mother's name, and filtered according to predefined exclusion criteria. Counts are presented separately for dengue virus (DENV; red), chikungunya virus (CHIKV; green), and Oropouche virus (OROV; blue) at each stage. Key differential patterns include: (i) absence of negative RT-PCR exclusions for OROV, reflecting universal testing during emergence response versus routine sampling for DENV/CHIKV; (ii) higher absolute unmatched records for OROV (n = 7706), consistent with larger notification volume during epidemic peak, though proportional rates were comparable (DENV 25·2%, CHIKV 19·4%, OROV 38·3% of merged records); and (iii) similar proportions of missing Ct values across viruses (0·25–0·62%). The final analytical dataset comprised 10,793 infections: 4058 DENV, 2508 CHIKV, and 4227 OROV.

figures.label: Fig. 2
figures.caption: Temporal trends, spatial distribution, and age-specific incidence of arboviral infections, 2024–2025. (A) Weekly distribution of reported cases of chikungunya virus (CHIKV), dengue virus (DENV), and Oropouche virus (OROV) by epidemiological week in 2024–2025. Bars represent the proportion of total notified cases attributed to each virus per week. (B) Municipality-level incidence rates (cases per 100,000 inhabitants) for OROV (blue), DENV (red), and CHIKV (green). Choropleth maps depict the spatial distribution of each virus; municipalities with missing data are shown in grey. (C) Age-specific incidence rates (per 100,000 inhabitants) by sex for each virus, presented as population pyramids. Incidence was calculated using population denominators from the 2022 national census.

figures.label: Fig. 3
figures.caption: Forest plot of clinical and demographic features associated with arboviral infections. Panels show adjusted odds ratios (95% CI) derived from multinomial logistic regression models comparing DENV versus OROV, CHIKV versus OROV, and CHIKV versus DENV. All variables included in the model are presented. Values shown are n/N (number of patients with the symptom or characteristic over total cases for each arboviral infection). The vertical dashed line indicates the null value (OR = 1).

figures.label: Fig. 4
figures.caption: Cross-sectional temporal dynamics, distribution, and clinical associations of viral RNA levels across arboviral infections. Panels A–C show Ct value cross-sectional summaries of Ct values by day since symptom onset (left) and distributions of Ct values at sampling (right) for (A) Oropouche virus (OROV), (B) dengue virus (DENV), and (C) chikungunya virus (CHIKV). Each point represents the median Ct value among different individuals sampled on the corresponding day after symptom onset; these data do not represent longitudinal measurements within the same patients. Point size proportional to the number of samples; shaded areas indicate interquartile ranges (IQRs), and dashed lines represent fitted trends from generalized additive models. Increasing Ct values over time indicate declining viral RNA levels. Histograms display the distribution of Ct values across all samples for each virus. Panel D presents adjusted regression coefficients (β) and 95% confidence intervals describing the association between standardised Ct values (z-scores) and clinical domain scores. Estimates were obtained from multivariable linear regression models adjusted for age, sex, and time since symptom onset, with the latter modelled using restricted natural cubic splines (3 degrees of freedom). The vertical dashed line indicates the null effect (β = 0). Filled circles indicate associations that remained statistically significant after false discovery rate (FDR) correction, whereas open circles indicate non-significant associations.
